t: How To Bring Instant Calm To Your Classroom https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/09/29/how-to-bring-instant-calm-to-your-classroom/
q: One of the biggest causes of misbehavior is excitability. It’s also one of the hardest to fix.

The good news is that once it’s identified, once it’s determined to be the root cause of silliness, rambunctiousness, and the like, it can be corrected almost instantly with the following five strategies.
One sure way to sweep out the negative vibes is to breathe, long and slow, deep through the abdomen. Relax your body and let your calm presence fill the room and carry from one student to the next.
The solution is to stop and stand in one place , especially when giving instructions or providing important information. This will draw eyes and ears to you.
If you can cut your talking by one third, you’ll notice a dramatic difference in attentiveness. Your students will have time to process, ponder, and comprehend.
But they must become not merely strategies you try once in a while or when things get particularly chaotic. Rather, they must become as much a part of your classroom as the desks and chairs.
x: Linsin identifies excitability as one of the most common and hardest-to-notice causes of misbehavior, since teachers immersed in it daily often stop perceiving it while a visitor feels it instantly.
The five strategies must become permanent classroom habits, not occasional fixes used only when a class becomes chaotic.
Five specific strategies are offered to reduce excitability: breathe, pause, stop moving, reduce talking, and slow down overall pace.
Standing still while giving instructions is said to draw student eyes and ears away from environmental distractions.
Cutting teacher talk time by roughly a third is claimed to produce a dramatic improvement in student attentiveness.
The five strategies must become permanent classroom habits, not occasional fixes used only when a class becomes chaotic.

t: The Secret Skills of Master Teachers: Paul Graham and the Right Kind of Procrastination astination/
q: There are three variants of procrastination, depending on what you do instead of working on something: you could work on (a) nothing, (b) something less important, or (c) something more important. That last type, I'd argue, is good procrastination.

The most dangerous kind, Graham says, is “unconscious type-B” procrastination — because here it feels like we're being productive, we're making lists and checking them off — but we're actually just managing the constant stream of urgent things that come our way, keeping work on important things always beyond our reach.
Productivity, Graham argues, can be its own form of bad procrastination when we're being productive with unimportant things.

The first thing is to be asking the right question. I've written about this a bit here, but the gist is this: it's all about long-term flourishing. How do we best promote the long-term flourishing of young people in our schools? (“Best,” of course, meaning that we have to find ways that are efficient and sustainable versus ways that burn out teachers every year and eventually drive them to quit.)

The thing is, Graham's type-C procrastination does have costs. For example, when we neglect to respond to someone's email for days, simply because we've not checked email, it can harm our relationship with that person.

But neglecting the inbox today means that I write four blog posts in a few hours, each of which gets to live on the Internet indefinitely doing who knows what good, unleashing who knows which educator into type-C procrastination on the big, pressing questions of our time.
x: Graham's three procrastination types (nothing, something less important, something more important) give teachers a diagnostic for where their time actually goes.
Feeling productive is the hazard: checking off lists of urgent but unimportant tasks is itself a form of bad procrastination.

Choosing what to neglect is justified by the question of long-term student flourishing, pursued sustainably rather than at the price of burnout.

t: The Secret Skills of Master Teachers: Making Bad Habits Harder and Ambiguous Habits Better uous-habits-clearer/
q: When my bad habits kick in — news reading, Twitter scrolling, YouTube watching, or stopping aimlessly into a colleague's room — I derail my chances, that precious hour, of doing the kind of work that will deepen my craft or improve the long-term flourishing outcomes of my classroom.

The trick here, as Eric Barker, author of Barking Up the Wrong Tree: The Surprising Science Behind Why Everything You Know About Success Is (Mostly) Wrong, aptly summarizes, is making bad habits “a pain in the ass to do.” The harder a bad habit is, the quicker it will stop being a habit.

The first three bad habits I listed are the kinds of things where my brain gets to switch itself into passive mode and feed a craving. Afterwards, I find myself in a place where my mood is typically worse, and I'm not much smarter for it.
Sometimes, impromptu drop-ins like this have created the strong social bonds that make working where I work a richer and much more rewarding experience.

But then there are probably an equal number of impromptu collegial conversations that have devolved into complaining or left me anxious or otherwise used up deep work time in return for minimal relational gain.
I think the key here is, when we do drop in (or get dropped in on), we have to own up to our role in keeping the conversation productive.

When we limit our availability for impromptu drop-ins, sure, we do miss out on some good things, but we also save up the mental and relational energy it takes, when we do converse with colleagues, to keep things oriented in the right directions.
x: Stuart turns from outside interruptions to the teacher's own autopilot habits, such as news reading, Twitter and YouTube, which derail the deep non-instructional work of teaching.
Following Eric Barker, he argues the way to break a bad habit is to make it a pain to do, and he describes concrete friction like a ten-minute browser limit and no social apps on his phone.
Bad habits are defined by outcome: they leave the teacher no closer to improving the classroom or his own sanity.
Adding friction (time-capped browser extensions, no social apps on the phone) works better than relying on willpower.
Aimless colleague drop-ins are ambiguous, since they can build bonds and insight or devolve into complaining and lost deep-work time.
Limiting availability has a cost in lost good moments but preserves energy for more productive conversations.

t: 3 Simple Ways To Check For Understanding
q: In observing teachers, one common area of weakness is checking for understanding. Not every teacher, of course. But many.
Often, the most I hear from teachers is “Are there any questions?” Which just doesn’t cut it.
Whiteboards give you all the information you need to decide whether to begin independent work right away or continue teaching.
The way it works is that you’ll ask them not if they understand, but if they don’t understand.
This puts the onus on them, makes them responsible to speak up, and leaves them with no excuse not to do the work.
They bring silence, instill true independence, and trigger the highly pleasurable flow state, where students get lost in their work.
x: Failing to check for understanding before independent work is identified as a common weakness that leads to reteaching, boredom, and learned helplessness.

He rejects the vague, commonly used question 'Are there any questions?' and instead offers three low-tech, fast techniques: individual whiteboards that students hold up on signal to show their answers.
'Negative questions' work by shifting the burden of speaking up onto students rather than the teacher guessing who is confused.

t: The Secret Skills of Master Teachers: Reducing Distractions from Students
q: To produce the clarity of thought necessary for deep and impactful teaching, the teacher has to do something that her environment constantly resists: she must avail herself of distraction-free blocks of time each day in which to do her most important work.

My classroom is at the end of a hallway in our small town high school. When I'm not teaching, there are 120 kids on my total roster (this year), and approximately 360 additional kids in the 10th, 11th, and 12th grade whom I've taught previously. That's 480 kids every day in the building who know where my room is, know me, and might decide that it's worth stopping by to say hi or ask a question or tell me a Star Wars joke or any number of other nice but distracting things.

Well, no. Schools don't exist primarily so that young people can develop relationships with adults who have chosen to spend their lives perpetually in school. We cultivate relationships with students so that we might optimally promote their long-term good — as that, and not relationships, is actually what school is “all about.
It's the long-term flourishing of kids — not relationships with the kids. Relationships serve that ultimate end.

So, I've found that I can actually cultivate adequate and even impactful relationships with students through brief, focused moments of genuine connection before, during, or after class. Additionally, I can work to love my students and affirm them, as my grandfather used to do for us grandkids. I can get their names right quickly and remember their birthdays using simple techniques. There are plenty of tools for building strong relationships with students within narrow time constraints.

But it's a critical mistake — one that I made for years — to leave my door open at all times — before school, during prep, after school — like some kind of magnet for the 480 kids in our high school who, at any given time, might want to come and say hi. The numbers there work out to me being interrupted constantly, every single day, during times at which I'd be doing greater service to the school and its kids by focusing on the six things that matter most, or planning the next unit, or giving fast feedback on student work.
So instead of the open door all the time, mine is a closed door mostly, and when it's closed I'm hiding in a back corner of my classroom with the work at hand.
x: Stuart argues that deep, impactful teaching requires distraction-free blocks of time, and that the teacher's own environment works against this.
He anticipates the objection that teaching is about relationships and answers that relationships are a means to students' long-term flourishing, not the end of schooling.
Stuart reframes relationships as serving long-term student flourishing rather than being the purpose of school.
He anticipates the objection that teaching is about relationships and answers that relationships are a means to students' long-term flourishing, not the end of schooling.
Brief, focused moments of connection before, during and after class can build adequate relationships, so he keeps his door mostly closed and works in a back corner.
Leaving the door open before school, during prep and after school was, by his own account, a critical mistake he made for years.
His practical fix is a mostly closed door and a quiet corner for focused work.

t: Why Picking Your Battles Is Bad Advice
q: When it comes to classroom management, you’ve got to pick your battles. So the advice goes.
This is a big mistake. Picking your battles is terrible advice. It amounts to a bottoming of standards, a surrendering of your beliefs and values, and a giving in and giving up on students.
You see, it’s the small, seemingly inconsequential details that protect you from the big things—the major disruptions, the dramatic incidents, the endless stress.
A talkative lesson or a lazy routine isn’t a sign that your students can’t do any better.

Taking a stand on the little things is the secret to impeccable behavior. It’s in holding students accountable for how they enter your classroom or take out their laptops or work independently that keeps disrespect and unruliness from ever entering the picture.
This doesn’t mean that you have to fight every battle. It means that you don’t fight any battle at all. Instead, you simply follow through on your promises .
x: Linsin pushes back against the common advice to 'pick your battles,' which he characterizes as a lowering of standards that amounts to inconsistency—unfair to students and a driver of increasing misbehavior.

Linsin pushes back against the common advice to 'pick your battles,' which he characterizes as a lowering of standards that amounts to inconsistency—unfair to students and a driver of increasing misbehavior.
Small, seemingly minor details—like how backpacks are hung or groups are formed—are framed as the actual protection against major disruptions, via the broken windows theory.

When a lesson turns talkative or a routine gets sloppy, he contends this is not evidence that expectations should be lowered but a signal that teachers should ask for more, not less, through re-teaching and greater explicitness.
Insistence on small procedural details is presented as the secret to impeccable behavior and lasting classroom peace.
The recommended approach isn't fighting every battle, but consistently following through on stated expectations so no true battle ever arises.

t: A Fun Way To Teach Students How Not To Behave https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/09/08/a-fun-way-to-teach-students-how-not-to-behave/
q: One of the most effective classroom management strategies is teaching students how not to behave .
It’s an effective strategy because when students see themselves in your modeling, they become less likely to repeat the behavior. The reason is that it strikes a nerve atop their personal pride.
One of the keys to making the strategy work is to have fun with it. It’s your exaggeration and humor that cause students to rethink taking part in the behavior again.
The solution is to personify the behavior in an imaginary student. When it’s attributed to someone who doesn’t exist—Bobo or Lulu, for example—then it naturally adds a lightheartedness to the lesson.
It’s fun. But more than anything, it makes the how-not strategy more effective. It keeps the tone upbeat and less personal—as you’ll never single out a specific student.
Your students will know that beneath the humor . . . Beats the heart of a leader that accepts nothing less than their very best.
x: Even high school students respond well to this approach when they trust the teacher, and it must be paired with genuine follow-through on the classroom management plan.

Because students recognize themselves in the modeling, it strikes at their pride and makes the behavior feel awkward or embarrassing, especially when delivered with exaggeration and humor rather than lecture.

Attributing the behavior to an imaginary student (e.g., 'Bobo' or 'Lulu') keeps the exercise lighthearted and avoids singling out real students.

q: The Mensch [teacher] has a tremendous willingness to learn from everything and everyone. He or she seeks feedback and is not blindsided by unexplored weaknesses.

To be the kind of teacher from whom great teaching tends to flow, the internal work is where it's at. A piece of this work is, I think, the exploration of one's weaknesses, as Martinuzzi suggests above.

One of the weaknesses I want to explore in myself this school year is my tendency to live in a state we all know: Survival Mode. Last minute lessons, morning-of trips to the copier, constantly feeling as if we're just catching up.

A sliver of my weakness is procrastination — letting my work time slip into time-wasting pursuits like unconstrained news reading, or “real quick” Twitter checks, or undisciplined email management. That last one is tricky because email is something I need to do thoughtfully — after all, there are dignified human beings on the other ends of many of those messages — but it's also something that I can use as a means for procrastinating.

But it's far from the whole. I suspect a huge additional part is that I still say yes to too many things: too many meetings, too many efforts that I support, too many extended conversations with colleagues I admire.
The work continues then — joyfully so. It is a great delight to find the areas in which one must improve. How terribly boring all of this would otherwise be.
x: He proposes three questions - where am I weak, what's beneath that weakness, how can I improve - and then models them on himself in public.

The weakness he names is Survival Mode: last-minute lessons, morning-of copier runs, the permanent sense of catching up.
Procrastination is one strand, and he is candid that email is the hardest case because it is both real work owed to real people and a convenient escape from writing or planning.
He proposes three questions - where am I weak, what's beneath that weakness, how can I improve - and then models them on himself in public.
The closing reframe is worth keeping: finding the areas where one must improve is treated as a delight rather than an indictment, which is what makes the examination repeatable.

t: How To Avoid Labeling Difficult Students
q: Difficult students feel different from their classmates. As if, they don’t quite fit in.
And yet, the most common advice given to teachers to help these students only makes matters worse.

It’s common for teachers to pull difficult students aside to cajole, pep-talk , and otherwise try to convince them to behave. But the deeper and far stronger message they get from you is that they’re not like all the rest, who you don’t pull aside.
Nothing tells a student they’re different and less able than a behavior contract.
These efforts to improve behavior, which many difficult students have been subject to for years and years, merely strengthen the limiting beliefs they have about themselves.
Be the one teacher to say “Enough is enough, and I believe in you.” Create a new prophecy for them to fulfill.
x: Difficult students already feel different from peers, and Linsin argues common 'helpful' interventions actually reinforce that label.
Difficult students already feel different from peers, and Linsin argues common 'helpful' interventions actually reinforce that label.
Five practices are named to stop: pulling students aside for pep-talks, using proximity control, fussing over them, behavior contracts, and privately negative thinking.
Each practice, he argues, communicates to the student and the class that this student is fundamentally different and less capable, which becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
These practices are said to create a self-fulfilling prophecy in which students internalize the belief that they're incapable of self-control.
